Posted May 17, 2002
Analysis by Richard Cowan

My friend and colleague, Pete Brady, has an article on the Cannabis Culture web site,

I would like to offer an alternative view.

I didn't call any of my friends in the coffee shop business, but rather I talked to my friends who are active in the Dutch anti-prohibitionist movement. They are much less concerned, and I think that they are right.

Dutch politics are sometimes difficult for even the Dutch to understand. The best place to get a little background on this is the

It is true that

First, understand that the coffee shop system developed under the Christian Democrats who until 8 years ago -- had been the dominant party in Holland since World War II. During all that time they were also nominally prohibitionist.

Moreover, the outgoing Social Democratic Prime Minister, Wim Kok, is also a prohibitionist. I have been told by very reliable sources that he never understood the coffee shop system, and his government reduced the amount of cannabis that could be purchased at one time from 30 grams to 5. They also raised the minimum age from 16 to 18, which was a major mistake.

In fairness, I should note that they did raise the permissible inventory levels from the absurd 30 gram limit to a more realistic 500 grams.

Second, the Christian Democrats will have only 43 out of 150 seats in new the Parliament. This means that they have to put together a coalition with other parties, but that may be very difficult. The party of the assassinated Pim Fortuyn (pronounced Peem For-town) which has 26 seats -- is more or less to the " right of center, " and therefore a logical coalition partner, but Fortuyn was in favor of legalization of cannabis.

Although Fortuyn was best known for his opposition to more immigration into Holland, he was very openly gay, and consequently very libertarian on social issues. The new head of his party, Mat Herben, has said that he will be true to Fortuyn's principles.

On the other hand, Balkende has never made closing the coffee shops a priority issue, and not everyone in his own party shares his views.

But from here it gets even more complicated. Assuming that the Christian Democrats can work out a deal with the Fortuyn party, they are still 6 votes short of a bare minimum majority, and it is not certain that the political novices in the Fortuyn group will follow party discipline.

But where are they going to get the six votes they need to have a nominal majority? The center right party, which was a part of the defeated coalition, has 23 seats, but is reluctant to join. The small right-wing religious parties have a combined projected win of 8 seats, but they are not very compatible even with the Christian Democrats, much less the Fortuyn party. And the other parties are all left of center.

In the past, with much less confusing situations, it has sometimes taken months to work out a coalition. In the end, that may be impossible to do, and so there may be a minority government, and elections again sometime next year. Nothing will be done about cannabis policy during that time.

And then there is the way that things really work in Holland. Control of the coffee shops is at the municipal level and most of the cities of Holland are in favor of the coffee shop system, as are most of the police.
See

Two years ago, by a majority of one, the Dutch parliament voted to " legalize " the supply of coffee shops. This was done at the urging of the mayors of the cities. The vote was not binding on the government, but the underlying situation has not changed.

Then there is the situation in the rest of Europe. A few years ago the Dutch were alone, but the disastrously counterproductive nature of cannabis prohibition has become more and more obvious to other European countries. Next year the Swiss are very likely to vote for the de facto legalization of cannabis, including the supply. The French political situation is in a state of confusion, but next month there will be parliamentary elections. It is likely that the French will continue to move away from cannabis prohibition. There are similar moves in other countries, and cannabis prohibition is collapsing in the UK.
See

In this context, it is even more unlikely that any Dutch government would seriously try to close the coffee shops. And of course, the fact that the cannabis business is a huge money maker for Holland is not lost on that very business oriented country.

Then finally there is what I call " the Nol van Schaik factor. " Nol owns

It isn't as though the coffee shops would just close without huge protests. The political costs would be enormous and there is no mandate to take such drastic action; nor do the Dutch have the blood lust that it would take to suppress the cannabis movement.

In fact, if the worst happened, they would just go back to the old " house dealer " system, which is how the coffee shops began. The Dutch have " been there, done that, " so I really don't think that they are going back.

But -- especially if you have never been there-- by all means go to Holland and support our friends there this summer. Everyone will be the better for it.
